messages.author: 5a1b5a9591c118ef
messages.subject: secondary x axis
parts:
Dear all,

I know this has been asked before, but I couldn't find a solution in
the archives or the manual.

I need to have a secondary axis in my graph (at the top, say, with
custom labels and custom positions). It's not meaningless (imho) and
hardly confusing as the two axes are simply a different scale for the
same quantity (wavelength and frequency), similar to a problem asked
last year involving Celcius and Fahrenheit scales. Even if it was an
evil idea (which, in this particular case, I don't think it is), I
have to do it anyway to please the reader.

I found the guide_axis internal function in the code of ggplot2, but I
fail to place the grob in the correct coordinates system and position.

qplot(1:10,1:10)
grid.draw(guide_axis(at = c(0, 1, 2, 3), labels = paste(letters[c(0,
1, 2, 3)]), position="top", theme=theme_bw()))

I'm extremely impressed by this last version of ggplot2 both by the
clarity and the level of customization, but I'll have to revert to
lattice if I can't get this to work.

Best regards,

baptiste

messages.author: b26ea422f70d3a1f
messages.subject: Re: secondary x axis
parts:
Baptiste,

As a worst-case workaround, I have noticed that labels= will accept the " " newline character. You could do something like:

qplot (x, y) + scale_x_continuous("X Stuff", breaks=c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0), labels=c("12 13", "10 15", "5 12", "20 04"))

to get apparently two numbers at each tick mark. So in your example of Celusius and Farenheit, you'd have to make one the primary item (nice even numbers) and derive the second at the same points (would not be nice even numbers).

Just a thought

Wayne

Well the bad news is that chapter is a bit out of date, after changes
I made to get facet_wrap working (you can always use grid.ls to see
what the current system is). However, even had the examples worked, I
don't think it would have got you much closer to a drawing a secondary
axis - what you really need to be able to do is modify the viewports
which is currently not possible with grid.

I agree that for this situation a secondary axis does make sense, but
I haven't given any thought to how it would work. How would you
specify the relationship between the two axes? How would it work with
respect to free scales? It would also need substantial changes to the
facet layout, and that code is already pretty complex. None of this
is to say that it will never happen, just that it is rather low on
priority list currently.

Regards,

Hadley

Hi Hadley,

Thanks for your answer. I understand this is a very low priority, but
I'd happily settle for a dirty work-around as it's only a one-time
graph that I need to produce. Below is a realistic example, in base
graphics and in lattice graphics (where it's already kind of a tweak,
imho).

L2eV <- # converts wavelength to energy
function (lambda)
{
cel <- 299792458
h <- 6.62606896e-34
ee <- 1.602176487e-19
eV <- h * cel/ee/lambda
eV
}

valuesLambda<-c(400,500,600,700,800,1000)*1e-3 # custom values for the
second axis
valuesL2eV<- L2eV(valuesLambda*1e-6) # corresponding positions in the
plot units

my.data <- data.frame(energy <- seq(1, 3, length=100), y = (energy)^2)

### base graphics ###

with(my.data, {
plot(energy, y, t="l",xlab=expression("resonance energy / eV"),
ylab=expression("resonance width / eV"))
axis(3, at=valuesL2eV ,labels = paste(valuesLambda))
mtext(expression("wavelength / "*mu*m), line=2)
})


### lattice graphics ###
xyplot(y~energy, data=my.data, t="l", scales=list(y=list(tck=c(1, 0)),
x=list(tck=c(1, 0))),
par.settings = list(layout.widths = list(ylab = 1,axis.right= 1.5),
layout.heights = list(xlab = 1,axis.top= 1.5)) ,
xlab=expression("resonance energy / eV"), ylab=expression("resonance
width / eV"),
panel = function(x, y, ...) {
panel.xyplot(x, y, ...)
cpl <- current.panel.limits()
pushViewport(viewport(xscale = cpl$xlim,
yscale = cpl$ylim,
clip = "off"))
## put anything you want unclipped inside this:
panel.axis("top", outside=T, at=valuesL2eV,
labels = paste(valuesLambda), rot=0)
panel.text(x=mean(cpl$xlim), y=max(cpl$ylim) , expression
("wavelength / "*mu*m), pos=3, offset=2)
## end of unclipped part
upViewport()
})

#My best shot in ggplot2 (not even close to working)

p <- qplot(1:10, 1:10)
pushViewport(viewport(name="main", layout=grid.layout(nrow = 2, ncol =
1 ,
widths=unit(6, "inches"),
heights=unit(c(1, 4), "inches"))))
pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.col=1, layout.pos.row=1,
just="center",
name = "top"))
grid.xaxis()
upViewport()
pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.col=1, layout.pos.row=2,
just="center",
name = "bottom"))
print(p, newpage=FALSE, vp="bottom")
upViewport()


Any help would be very much appreciated!

Baptiste

messages.author: b26ea422f70d3a1f
messages.subject: Re: secondary x axis
parts:
Two observations:

David: in your example, how would the grid lines work? I assume we
want two scales but only one set of grid lines that would align with
only one of the scales. My feeling would be that this would require
major changes to scales, which probably currently assume that they
"own" the background grid lines.

Hadley: could a secondary "scale" be implemented as a kind of fancy
axis label expression instead of an actual scale_*?

ALSO, I like how ggplot2 has the smallest margins around graphs (and
hence the max graph area) of the three. However, I just tried the
example from the book that uses an expression with frac() in it and
the numerator of the fraction y-axis label gets chopped off.

Wayne

messages.author: 5a1b5a9591c118ef
messages.subject: Re: secondary x axis
parts:
Dear all,

Thank you for the suggestions. It seems to me that the easiest
solution
would be to consider the second axis as an external object added for
convenience, much like raw grid commands can be used to fine-tune
lattice
and ggplot2 graphs (for instance, the example of an arrow joining two
lattice plots in the lattice book). It just doesn't fit in the general
paradigm of ggplot2, and I don't think there will ever be a need for a
general function that blends in well with all cases.

Personally, I'd be more than happy with the following situation:

- create a graph with ggplot2

(- possibly enlarge the margins around the plot. I don't think this is
much
of a problem, one can always print the graph in a grid layout)

- navigate to the viewport containing the data

- draw a raw grid object *in this native coordinate system* (the
particular
grob, i can create myself, no need for Hadley to worry about its
possible
bugs or ugliness)


It is clearly not necessary to use such tweaks in 99% of the graphs
(ggplot=
2
provides almost every possible object in a consistent framework), but
there
are always cases where I need a custom addition to the graph (and the
only
way I can see at the moment is to use Illustrator and draw things
manually... far from ideal!

In some cases, it may even be an idea to share such custom
"intermediate
level" grobs in an add-on package "ggplot2Extra".

Does this make sense?

baptiste
